reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Weedon's Skin Pathology
clinicalPearls: Amyloid deposition confined to the skin without systemic or visceral involvement, distinct from systemic amyloidosis
Lichen amyloidosis presents as intensely pruritic, hyperkeratotic, brownish papules that coalesce into rippled plaques, classically on the shins and extensor legs
Macular amyloidosis produces rippled or reticulate greyish-brown hyperpigmentation, typically over the interscapular back, often linked to chronic friction from towels or brushes
In the keratinic (lichen and macular) forms the amyloid is derived from degenerate epidermal keratinocytes, staining for cytokeratins, and is closely tied to chronic scratching and friction

Nodular amyloidosis is different: it is a localised AL-type deposit produced by a clonal population of cutaneous plasma cells and carries a small risk of progression to systemic amyloidosis, warranting follow-up
Familial primary cutaneous amyloidosis is associated with variants in OSMR and IL31RA, and lichen or macular amyloidosis may occur in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A
Management focuses on breaking the itch-scratch cycle with topical corticosteroids, antipruritics and phototherapy, since persistent friction perpetuates the deposition
reference.pathophysiology: Primary cutaneous amyloidosis involves extracellular deposition of amyloid restricted to the dermis. In the common keratinic forms (lichen and macular amyloidosis), chronic friction and scratching are thought to cause apoptosis (filamentous degeneration) of basal keratinocytes; the resulting keratin fragments are converted into amyloid within the papillary dermis, which is why the deposits stain for cytokeratins and the disorder is perpetuated by the itch-scratch cycle. Genetic susceptibility, including variants in the oncostatin M receptor (OSMR) and interleukin-31 receptor (IL31RA) in familial disease, contributes in some patients. Nodular amyloidosis differs fundamentally, arising from local production of immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloid by a clonal infiltrate of cutaneous plasma cells.
additionalDifferentials: Lichen simplex chronicus and prurigo nodularis
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and other pigmentary disorders in macular disease
Nodular basal cell carcinoma or adnexal tumour in the nodular form
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with Congo red staining showing apple-green birefringence under polarised light
Immunohistochemistry for cytokeratins to identify keratin-derived amyloid in the keratinic forms
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation, particularly for nodular amyloidosis to exclude systemic disease
Serum free light chains where AL amyloid is suspected
Assessment for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A when there is a suggestive family history
Long-term monitoring of nodular amyloidosis for progression to systemic amyloidosis
redFlags: Features of systemic amyloidosis such as macroglossia, cardiac or renal involvement or a monoclonal paraprotein
Nodular lesions with a demonstrable clonal plasma cell population or paraproteinaemia
Rapidly changing or ulcerating nodules suggesting an alternative neoplasm
Associated symptoms suggesting multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A
reference.prognosis: Primary cutaneous amyloidosis is benign and does not itself shorten life, but the keratinic forms tend to be chronic and troublesome because of persistent pruritus. Nodular amyloidosis is usually localised yet requires surveillance, as a minority progress to systemic amyloidosis.
pitfalls: Assuming all cutaneous amyloid is benign and failing to investigate and monitor the nodular form for systemic progression
Not recognising that persistent scratching and friction drive and perpetuate the keratinic forms
Missing an associated systemic amyloidosis when cutaneous deposits are in fact secondary
Overlooking the association of lichen and macular amyloidosis with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A
Attributing interscapular pigmentation to post-inflammatory change without considering macular amyloidosis
management: Break the itch-scratch cycle with topical or intralesional corticosteroids and antipruritics including topical agents and antihistamines
Use emollients and advise avoidance of friction from towels and brushes that perpetuate the keratinic forms
Consider phototherapy with ultraviolet B, or topical or systemic retinoids, for refractory lichen and macular disease
Manage nodular amyloidosis with surgical excision or laser and maintain long-term surveillance for progression to systemic amyloidosis using protein electrophoresis and free light chains
Screen for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A when the family history or features are suggestive
Offer genetic counselling in familial disease associated with OSMR and IL31RA variants
